Violence chez les jeunes : à Rivière-des: Youth violence: in Rivière-des-Prairies, parents look for solutions
À Rivière-des-Prairies, parents et inter: In Rivière-des-Prairies, parents and community workers join forces to prevent youth violence and criminal recruitment.
Parents et intervenants réunis à Rivière: Parents and community workers gathered in Rivière-des-Prairies to discuss preventing juvenile delinquency. Photo: Nouri Nesrouche.
Le 9 mai dernier, j’ai assisté à une ren: On May 9, I attended a community meeting held in Rivière-des-Prairies and organized by Équipe RDP and the Fondation Marbens Dorelus. It focused on an issue affecting Montréal neighbourhoods: youth violence.
Ce sujet correspond à ce que nous essayo: This topic reflects what we try to document at La Converse: social issues that take shape in neighbourhoods, in direct contact with residents, families and organizations trying to act before situations become irreversible.
J’ai recueilli les échanges entre les in: I recorded the exchanges between community workers and the parents in attendance, and I asked questions of parents and of street-level community workers involved with young people in Rivière-des-Prairies.
J’ai également consulté différentes sour: I also consulted a range of public and institutional sources in order to place the meeting in a broader context: the rise in violence involving teenagers in Montréal, prevention strategies, and community initiatives put in place in the east end of the island.
Cet article est le résultat de ce travai: This article is the result of that fieldwork, which aims to report on a reality lived at the heart of the communities that bear its consequences.
<strong>Réunis autour d’intervenants com: Gathered with community workers and a family grieving a loss to gun violence, parents in Rivière-des-Prairies spoke frankly about juvenile delinquency, social media, criminal recruitment and family burnout. Beyond the alarming findings, the meeting was above all about regaining a collective reflex: to talk, to act and to rebuild ties before it is too late.
Le silence s’installe brusquement, puis: Silence suddenly falls, then tears spread through part of the room. At the chalet in Parc Armand-Bombardier in Rivière-des-Prairies, about thirty parents are taking part on Saturday, May 9, in a meeting on preventing youth delinquency, organized by<l1> Équipe RDP</l1> and the<l2> Fondation Marbens Dorelus</l2>.
Durant plus de deux heures, les échanges: For more than two hours, the discussion circles around a single question: how to keep teenagers from tipping into violence or becoming its victims.
Puis la mère de Marbens Dorelus, un jeun: Then the mother of Marbens Dorelus, a young man shot dead in Anjou in July 2025, tries to speak. Quickly overcome with emotion, she struggles to finish her sentences, then soon gives up. In the circle formed by the participants, several women wipe away tears. One of them breaks down. The emotional weight reflects the depth of a phenomenon that now reaches beyond the communities directly affected by shootings.
« Nous vivons dans un contexte où nos je: “We live in a context where our young people are facing difficult realities,” Kingslyne Toussaint, executive director of Équipe RDP, said in her opening remarks, citing violence, dropping out of school and the effects on mental health.
<strong>« Les jeunes vivent dans un mond: “Young people live in a parallel world”
La rencontre se tient alors que plusieur: The meeting comes as a number of Montréal neighbourhoods, particularly in the east end of the island, have been marked in recent years by shootings, arson, vehicle thefts and conflicts involving teenagers or very young adults. Just this past Thursday, May 14, a teenager was stabbed in front of a high school in Saint-Henri.
Lors d’une sortie médiatique le 10 févri: At a press conference on February 10, Montréal police (SPVM) chief Fady Dagher welcomed the<l1> 52% drop in the gun violence rate since 2021</l1>, while acknowledging that the sense of insecurity expressed by many Montrealers is entirely justified. Dagher also noted on that occasion that in 2026, his officers expect to encounter ever-younger teenagers involved in crimes, including crimes involving firearms.
À Rivière-des-Prairies, l’intervenant de: In Rivière-des-Prairies, street-level community worker Burt Pierre works daily with young people exposed to these realities. Tasked with setting the stage before the discussions, he painted a picture for the parents that he himself calls “alarming.” In his view, the current situation cannot be understood without going back to the episodes of gun violence that have marked Rivière-des-Prairies in recent years. Since 2017, he recalls, several incidents have shaken the neighbourhood, including an armed conflict that cost three members of the community their lives, two of them young boys.
L’intervenant décrit des<l1> adolescents: He describes<l1> teenagers approached online to take part in car thefts, acts of intimidation and arson</l1>. His observations in the field match those of the police. According to him, criminal recruitment starts earlier and earlier and now largely happens through social media. “It’s become cool to get into crime, so you’re going to meet more kids at a younger age,” he warns, because “it’s fun, there’s a lot of adrenaline [...] I’ve got kids I work with, it starts from age 12!”
C’est « cool », et en plus c’est payant,: It’s “cool,” and on top of that it pays, Pierre adds, citing a range of $5,000 to $25,000 that a young person can earn for a car theft job.
Face à cette montée des violences impliq: In the face of this rise in violence involving teenagers, governments and police forces have made a flurry of announcements since the pandemic. Quebec announced in March 2026 <l1>$1.9 million in funding for 11 Montréal youth programs</l1> aimed at preventing crime, while Ottawa has invested<l2> $5 million in fighting crime in Montréal</l2>. The SPVM also says it wants to intervene earlier with at-risk youth to keep them from sliding into lasting criminality.
Chargé d’animer la conversation, l’agent: Tasked with leading the conversation, mobilization officer Riguerre Antoine steers participants to go as deep as possible in their thinking and to avoid the shortcuts so often associated with youth violence. Burt Pierre insists: in his view, the problem cannot be reduced to a simple lack of parental supervision. “Many parents work 40, 50, sometimes 70 hours a week,” he says. “It’s not that they don’t want to be there.”
Dans la salle, plusieurs parents hochent: In the room, several parents nod, recognizing themselves in the portrait the community workers have drawn. Two mothers from Rivière-des-Prairies, interviewed after the event, describe a constant worry about adolescence. One of them tells La Converse that her son’s behaviour changed as soon as he started high school. “It’s like he drifted away,” she says. “So you have to go find out why.”
L’autre parle de la difficulté de concil: The other speaks of the difficulty of balancing parental supervision with financial pressure. “They tell parents to watch their kids, but at the same time, you have to work to provide for the family,” she says, then adds: “With the cost of living, we can’t always be everywhere.” The same mother talks about “a vicious circle,” because in her view, some teenagers end up seeking out for themselves the money or social status they feel they can’t get any other way.
Pendant la rencontre, plusieurs particip: During the meeting, several participants also decry the lack of resources in schools and community organizations. One mother says she had to find a private psychoeducator on her own after her son experienced bullying.
Pour certains intervenants, cette fragil: For some community workers, this fragility creates fertile ground for criminal recruitment. “Young people are looking for a sense of belonging,” Burt Pierre explains. “If the street becomes the place where they feel seen, protected or valued, it’s going to take that place.”
Après les présentations, le micro circul: After the presentations, the microphone passes freely among the parents. Several insist that they refuse to lose their children and that they are determined to stay mobilized despite their discouragement.
Une participante raconte qu’il devient d: One participant says it is becoming difficult to step in when a teenager is being disrespectful in the neighbourhood. “Sometimes you talk to a kid, and it’s the parents who come to blame you for intervening,” she sums up. For several participants, this loss of the collective reflex further weakens families.
Obenson Dorelus revient lui aussi sur ce: Obenson Dorelus also returns to this idea of shared responsibility, explaining that he grew up in an environment where many adults in the neighbourhood took part in raising children, because “it takes a whole village to raise a child,” he repeats.
Après la mort de son fils, il affirme av: After his son’s death, he says he wanted to turn his pain into community action. Today, the Fondation Marbens Dorelus seeks in particular to offer spaces for dialogue for parents, young people and community workers, advocating an approach centred on family support and prevention.
Au-delà des constats, la rencontre cherc: Beyond the findings, the meeting seeks to bring out possible courses of action. The Équipe RDP community workers stress the importance of street-level outreach, particularly in disadvantaged neighbourhoods. This approach guides, among other things, the<l1> Pivot project</l1>, rolled out in the east end of Montréal after the rise in gun violence seen during the pandemic. The program relies on a continuous presence with young people: at school, in sports activities, on the street and even in detention when necessary. “Being present everywhere young people risk falling into delinquency,” sums up one community worker, “before, during, after.”
Les intervenants défendent aussi une app: The community workers also advocate an approach inspired by public health, rather than a strictly punitive one. “Repression does part of the job, but it doesn’t do the whole job,” says Burt Pierre.
Pendant la rencontre, Burt Pierre décrit: During the meeting, Burt Pierre describes several strategies used to maintain a connection with teenagers: music workshops, one-on-one support, spaces accessible to young adults and employment support.
Mais la prévention passe d’abord par le: But prevention starts first in the family home and with parents’ vigilance. Those present at the chalet in Parc Armand-Bombardier are urged not to downplay the distress that teenagers report. “The street will always make room for a young person who feels rejected,” sums up Burt Pierre.
Ce dernier encourage notamment les paren: He notably encourages parents to take more interest in their children’s online lives, to stay involved in their comings and goings and to build ties with other families in the neighbourhood. “Sometimes, just picking a kid up after basketball can prevent something,” he explains.
L’objectif n’est pas seulement de préven: The goal is not only to prevent criminal acts, but also to offer concrete alternatives to teenagers who are looking for a place, recognition or a way out of precarity.
Au terme de cette conversation, aucune s: At the end of the conversation, no miracle solution had emerged. But for a few hours, parents, community workers and a grieving family tried to rebuild something that many say they see disappearing: a collective ability to step in before tragedies happen and become irreversible.
<strong>Des signes qui peuvent indiquer: Signs that may point to distress in a young person:
• Isolement soudain et/ou rupture avec l:
• Sudden isolation and/or a break with usual friends
• Major changes in behaviour or mood
• Declining grades or absenteeism
• Cash, clothing or expensive items of unclear origin
• Unusual secrecy around the phone or social media
• Anxiety, irritability or unusual fear of going out or coming home
• Frequent conflicts at home or gradually shutting down communication
<strong>Maintenir le dialogue avec son a: Keeping the dialogue open with your teenager:
• Poser des questions ouvertes plutôt qu:
• Ask open-ended questions rather than confronting or accusing
• Take an interest in your teen’s digital world, especially if they are on Snapchat and Telegram
• Use simple moments (rides, meals, activities) to talk without pressure
• Avoid downplaying bullying, a fear or a change in behaviour
• Stay in touch with the school, teachers and community workers in the neighbourhood
Les intervenants d’Équipe RDP recommande: Équipe RDP community workers recommend not waiting for a situation to worsen. A young person who receives unusual gifts, seems to be under outside pressure, suddenly changes who they hang out with or becomes very secretive may need help quickly.
L’objectif n’est pas d’abord de punir, m: The goal is not first and foremost to punish, but to understand what is happening and to rebuild a safety net around the young person.
<strong>Où demander de l’aide sans passe: Where to ask for help without going straight to the police:
• Organismes communautaires jeunesse du:
• Neighbourhood youth community organizations, such as Équipe RDP
• School staff, psychoeducators and social workers
• Youth centres (maisons des jeunes)
• Street-level outreach teams
• CLSCs or youth psychosocial services

À Rivière-des-Prairies, une rencontre or: In Rivière-des-Prairies, a meeting organized by Équipe RDP and the Fondation Marbens Dorelus brought together parents, community workers and relatives of gun violence victims to discuss juvenile delinquency in Montréal. The discussion covered the criminal recruitment of teenagers through social media, financial pressure on families, the lack of resources and the importance of prevention. Despite the emotion and the alarming findings, participants insisted on the need to strengthen community ties and to act early to keep young people from tipping into violence.
